paper_metadata.title: Quantum algorithm for credit valuation adjustments

summary: This paper proposes a gate-based quantum algorithm for CVA using engineered-likelihood-function amplitude estimation, with a reported noiseless quantum CVA value of 1.987e-5 versus a Monte Carlo benchmark of 5.599e-5 and a discretized benchmark of 1.223e-5 for the 4-qubit example. The resource model uses 13 logical qubits and 136 logical two-qubit gates per ELF layer, and the authors estimate quantum runtime of 4.9e5 s at 0.001% relative error versus 3.7e6 s classically, with crossover only at very high precision (about 0.0067% relative error).

experiments.description: Gate-based quantum algorithm for credit valuation adjustment (CVA) using engineered-likelihood-function amplitude estimation, with state preparation via either QCBM or MPS and controlled-rotation circuits (CRCA) as near-term alternatives to reversible logic synthesis.

algorithm.variant: Engineered likelihood function (ELF) amplitude estimation for CVA

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Time is encoded with m qubits where M=2^m discretized time points; asset price is encoded with n qubits where N=2^n discretized price values. The joint distribution P(s_j,t_i) is loaded into amplitudes over |i,j⟩. Three ancilla qubits store payoff, probability of default, and discount factor.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate CVA = M(1-R)CvCpCq * <xi|Pi|xi>, where Pi projects onto ancilla state |111> and |xi> is the prepared quantum state.

problem_instance.description: Single-asset European call CVA instance with geometric Brownian motion asset dynamics and discretized time/price grid.
problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Monte Carlo simulation with 10^5 stochastic paths to estimate the benchmark CVA and discretize the joint time-price distribution; price range chosen as [mu_hat-3 sigma_hat, mu_hat+3 sigma_hat] from simulated prices.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Exact simulation of the trained quantum circuit for the noiseless CVA value; classical benchmark from Monte Carlo with 10^5 paths; resource-estimation comparison against classical Monte Carlo runtimes across target relative errors.

quantum_resources.readout_fidelity: f^3_nc for the three-qubit projector in the resource model

hardware.framework: Orquestra / quantlib for classical benchmark; exact simulation of quantum circuit for noiseless quantum value

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Classical Monte Carlo used to generate target distribution for QCBM/MPS training and to benchmark CVA.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Bayesian amplitude estimation with engineered likelihood function; CVA recovered from estimated <A|O|A> or <xi|Pi|xi>.

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: not reported for ELF; QCBM/MPS training curves shown separately

results.unit: logical two-qubit gates per ELF layer

speedup_claims.caveats: The paper notes the practical runtime depends strongly on fault-tolerant overhead and hardware parameters; the asymptotic quadratic advantage is not directly demonstrated on hardware.

speedup_claims.factor: about 7.55x faster wall-clock at 0.001% relative error
speedup_claims.conditions: assuming all-to-all connectivity, physical gate error rate 10^-3, surface code distance 18, 1 microsecond cycle time
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a resource-model projection, not an experimental hardware result.

speedup_claims.conditions: same fault-tolerant hardware assumptions as above
speedup_claims.caveats: The crossover point is estimated from the paper's runtime model and is hardware-dependent.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(1/epsilon_S) in the ideal amplitude-estimation setting; resource model interpolates between O(1/epsilon) and O(1/epsilon^2) depending on noise
complexity_analysis.total_operations_quantum: M=136 logical two-qubit gates per ELF layer; 13 logical qubits in the sample-generation circuit
complexity_analysis.crossover_n: relative error approximately 0.0067% in the paper's runtime projection
complexity_analysis.wall_clock_quantum: 4.9e5 seconds for relative error 0.001% under the paper's assumed fault-tolerant hardware model
complexity_analysis.wall_clock_classical: 3.7e6 seconds for the same CVA instance on a single-core classical computer

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Relative error around 0.0067% in the paper's projection; the paper states quantum becomes faster only at very high accuracy
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Fault-tolerant surface-code hardware with distance 18, 13 logical qubits, 136 logical two-qubit gates per ELF layer, and very high gate fidelity assumptions
limiting_factors: Classical Monte Carlo is faster for errors larger than about 0.35%
Quantum advantage depends on very low target error and strong error correction overhead
State-preparation error dominates the observable error budget
Resource model assumes surface-code protection and high-fidelity logical gates

notes: num_qubits=13 and gate count=136 are reported for the ELF sample-generation circuit in the resource-estimation section; the paper also reports 4 logical qubits for the state-preparation toy instance and 7 qubits for the CRCA/RLS comparison, but the main resource-estimation circuit uses 13 logical qubits.

hardware.type inferred as simulator_other because the paper reports exact simulation for the noiseless quantum CVA value and a separate fault-tolerant resource model rather than execution on a real QPU.
circuit_depth not explicitly given as a single number for the full ELF circuit; only per-layer gate count and resource model are reported.
The paper explicitly states classical runtime is faster for relatively coarse accuracy and that quantum only overtakes at very high precision.
The reported quantum CVA value is 1.987e-5, with classical benchmark CVAMC = 5.599e-5 and discretized benchmark CVA(2) = 1.223e-5.

experiments.description: State-preparation subexperiment for the CVA joint time-price distribution using a Quantum Circuit Born Machine (QCBM).

algorithm.variant: Quantum Circuit Born Machine (QCBM) for loading the discretized joint distribution P(s_j,t_i)
algorithm.ansatz: 4-qubit hardware-efficient ansatz with single-qubit Rx/Rz layers and an entangling XX layer
algorithm.convergence_criteria: training until cost function converges / rescaled cost approaches zero

problem_formulation.encoding_details: 4 qubits encode the 2-bit time register and 2-bit price register for the discretized joint distribution over |i,j⟩.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Minimize clipped negative log-likelihood between generated distribution p_theta(x) and target distribution p_tg(x).

problem_instance.description: Single-asset CVA state-preparation task for the discretized joint distribution P(s_j,t_i) derived from geometric Brownian motion.

dataset_specification.distribution: log-normal price distribution at each time step

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Target distribution obtained from 10^5 Monte Carlo trajectories; price range set to [mu_hat-3 sigma_hat, mu_hat+3 sigma_hat] and binned into discrete states.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Training curve and histograms before/after training; KL divergence used as accuracy metric; comparison against MPS and RLS in gate counts and training iterations.

hardware.framework: hybrid quantum-classical training; exact simulator not explicitly named

implementation_details.transpilation_target: ion-trap native XX gates are mentioned for the ansatz
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Monte Carlo-generated target distribution and binning.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Compute KL divergence and compare learned distribution histograms to target.

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: monotonic decrease toward zero after rescaling

speedup_claims.conditions: hybrid training of a 4-qubit QCBM state-preparation circuit
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper reports training behavior and gate counts, but does not claim an asymptotic or empirical speedup for QCBM state preparation.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not assessed; no advantage claim is made for QCBM state preparation alone
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: 4 qubits, 14 variational parameters, 2-layer ansatz with Rx/Rz single-qubit rotations and XX entangling gates
limiting_factors: Only a toy 4-qubit instance is shown
No runtime advantage over classical methods is demonstrated
Used as a subroutine for state preparation rather than a standalone application benchmark

notes: The paper reports the QCBM ansatz structure, 4 qubits, 14 gates, and 2 layers; it does not report a real QPU run, so hardware.type is inferred as simulator_other / hybrid training context.
The paper reports training iterations and KL divergence qualitatively, but not a formal asymptotic speedup claim for this subexperiment.
The paper presents QCBM as one of two state-preparation methods and reports training accuracy, not quantum advantage.
The comparison is against MPS and RLS in circuit cost and training behavior, not against a classical end-to-end solver.

experiments.description: State-preparation subexperiment for the CVA joint time-price distribution using a Matrix Product State (MPS) model and its circuit embedding.

algorithm.variant: Matrix Product State (MPS) state preparation for the discretized joint distribution P(s_j,t_i)
algorithm.ansatz: MPS with maximum bond dimension D=2
algorithm.convergence_criteria: stop when KL divergence threshold reached, objective improvement below threshold, or max iterations reached

problem_formulation.encoding_details: MPS prepares amplitudes over the n+m qubit basis states |i,j⟩ representing time and price bins.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Minimize negative log-likelihood L(A) = -(1/|S|) sum_{x in S} log p_A(x).

problem_instance.description: Single-asset CVA state-preparation task for the discretized joint distribution P(s_j,t_i).

dataset_specification.distribution: log-normal price distribution at each time step

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Target distribution obtained from Monte Carlo simulation and discretized over time/price bins.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Training time, KL divergence, and circuit-gate estimates reported for multiple qubit counts; comparison against QCBM and RLS.

hardware.framework: hybrid quantum-classical training; exact simulator not explicitly named

implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Convert trained MPS to quantum circuit via SVD/isometry decomposition; compare KL divergence and gate counts.

speedup_claims.caveats: The paper reports asymptotic circuit-preparation cost O(n D^2) and training times, but no direct quantum-vs-classical speedup claim.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(n D^2) two-qubit gates for circuit preparation from an MPS of bond dimension D
complexity_analysis.total_operations_quantum: For nqubits=4 and D=2, estimated 9 CNOTs and 19 single-qubit gates in the equivalent circuit

notes: The paper reports MPS training times and gate-count estimates, but not a real hardware execution; hardware.type is inferred as simulator_other / hybrid training context.
The asymptotic circuit-preparation cost O(n D^2) is explicitly stated in Appendix B.

experiments.description: Controlled-rotation subexperiment for CVA using the Controlled Rotation Circuit Ansatz (CRCA) as a near-term alternative to reversible logic synthesis.

algorithm.variant: Controlled Rotation Circuit Ansatz (CRCA) for approximating payoff, default probability, and discount-factor rotations
algorithm.ansatz: Sequential single-qubit rotation ansatz with Ry/Rz/Rx gates
algorithm.convergence_criteria: approximate target rotation functions; error measured by operator norm and 1-norm difference

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Discrete index register controls a single ancilla rotation implementing f(x_i) for each discretized input point.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Approximate R_f: |i>|0> -> |i>(sqrt(1-f(x_i))|0> + sqrt(f(x_i))|1>) for payoff/default/discount functions.

problem_instance.description: CVA subroutines for payoff, default probability, and discount factor on the 7-qubit CVA instance.
problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Functions discretized over the input register; exact function values used for comparison to CRCA approximation.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Compare CRCA against reversible logic synthesis in CNOT count and approximation error; report operator-norm error bounds and function-value error bounds.

implementation_details.classical_solver: reversible logic synthesis used as classical baseline for comparison
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Function discretization and exact RLS synthesis for baseline.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Compute operator-norm error and compare CNOT counts.

results.unit: CNOT gates for reversible logic synthesis baseline
operator-norm bound on state-preparation error contribution

speedup_claims.conditions: 7-qubit CVA instance; CRCA approximation for payoff, default probability, and discount factor
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a gate-count reduction, not a proven asymptotic speedup; classical optimization for CRCA becomes harder as qubit count grows.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(poly(n,m)) for exact reversible synthesis; CRCA is a shallower approximation with reduced CNOT count
complexity_analysis.total_operations_quantum: 36 CNOTs for the 4-qubit price register / 7-qubit CVA instance as reported
complexity_analysis.total_operations_classical: 89 CNOTs for RLS on the same 7-qubit CVA instance

notes: The paper reports the 7-qubit CVA instance and the CNOT counts for CRCA vs RLS, but not a hardware execution; hardware.type is inferred as simulator_other / synthesis study.
No formal asymptotic speedup claim is made for CRCA; it is presented as a near-term circuit-reduction heuristic.
